The filing (Apple Inc. fiscal 2025 Form 10-K, Item 1A and Item 3) ties four dated developments in calendar year 2025 to legal proceedings or government investigations involving Apple or its commercial partners:

**April 23, 2025 — EU Digital Markets Act (Item 3)**
- The European Commission fined Apple €500 million in its Article 5(4) noncompliance investigation and issued a cease-and-desist order requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions that prevent developers from steering users to distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple has appealed.
- The same day, the Commission issued preliminary findings in its separate Article 6(4) investigation (concerning Apple's new contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces). A final adverse determination could bring another cease-and-desist order and fines of up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales.

**April 30, 2025 — Epic Games litigation (Item 3)**
- The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California found Apple in violation of the 2021 anti-steering injunction, enjoined it from imposing any commission or fee on purchases consumers make outside an app, barred it from restricting or interfering with how developers direct consumers to external purchases, denied Apple's motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 injunction, and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are appropriate. Apple appealed to the Ninth Circuit.

**September 2, 2025 — Google search antitrust case (Item 1A)**
- The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia ordered remedies following its August 5, 2024 finding that Google — from which Apple earns search-licensing revenue — violated U.S. antitrust laws. **October 2025 — Epic Games appeal (Item 3)**
- The Ninth Circuit, having denied Apple's request for a stay but agreed to expedite the appeal, heard oral arguments in Apple's appeal of the April 30, 2025 ruling.

## Dividends on Boeing's 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock — dollar amounts in the 2024 Form 10-K

Excluding the 6.00% rate and the $1,000 per-share liquidation preference (and excluding the exhibits), the filing gives three distinct dollar amounts for dividends on this preferred stock:

**1. $72 million — Cash dividends declared on the preferred stock**
- This is the amount of dividends **declared** in December 2024. Per Note 19 (Shareholders' Equity), "dividends of $72 were declared to holders of record as of January 1, 2025, representing $12.50 per share, and were paid in cash on January 15, 2025."
- It also appears in the Consolidated Statements of Equity as "Cash dividends declared on Mandatory convertible preferred stock (72)," reducing retained earnings.

**2. $58 million — Preferred stock dividends accumulated during the period**
- This is the amount of dividends **accumulated** during 2024 (the cumulative-dividend accrual from the October 31, 2024 issuance through year-end). It appears in the Consolidated Statements of Operations, the segment data note, and Note 4 (Earnings Per Share) as the deduction used to arrive at "Net loss attributable to Boeing common shareholders": "Less: Mandatory convertible preferred stock dividends accumulated during the period 58."
- Note: The $72 million declared (for holders of record January 1, 2025) exceeds the $58 million accumulated through December 31, 2024, because the declared dividend covers the dividend period extending into January 2025.

**3. $345 million — Expected maximum annual cash dividends**
- In the "Risks Related to Financing and Liquidity" section, Boeing states: "We also expect to require **up to $345 million of cash per year** for the payment of dividends on the outstanding shares of our 6.00% Series A Mandatory Convertible Preferred Stock... through the mandatory conversion date of October 15, 2027." This is a forward-looking estimate of the annual cash cost if dividends are paid in cash.

### Summary
| Amount | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **$72 million** | Dividends declared in Dec 2024 (payable/paid in cash Jan 15, 2025); shown in Statements of Equity and Note 19 |
| **$58 million** | Dividends accumulated during 2024, deducted to compute net loss attributable to common shareholders (Statements of Operations, Note 4, segment note) |
| **$345 million** | Expected maximum cash required per year for preferred dividends through the Oct 15, 2027 mandatory conversion date (liquidity risk factor) |

(The related "$12.50 per share" declared-dividend figure is a per-share amount, not an aggregate dollar amount, and the $1,000 liquidation preference and 6.00% rate were excluded per your instructions.)

## Effects that occurred

1. **Blocked passage of products, services, and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine.**
   The filing states that "in response to the war in Ukraine, the United States and other jurisdictions imposed economic sanctions and export control measures which blocked the passage of our products, services and support into Russia, Belarus, and certain regions of Ukraine."

2. **NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia.**
   Both the Risk Factors and the MD&A state: "In fiscal year 2023, we stopped direct sales to Russia." (Direct sales to Russia in fiscal year 2022 were immaterial.)

3. **NVIDIA closed its business operations in Russia.**
   The filing states that "later in the year, we closed business operations in Russia."

4. **The war impacted end-customer sales in EMEA.**
   The Risk Factors section states: "Concurrently, the war in Ukraine has impacted end customer sales in EMEA." (The clause "and may continue to do so in the future" is a forward-looking risk and is excluded.)

## Effects the filing describes as possibly having occurred

5. **Revenue from partners that sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted.**
   The MD&A states: "Our revenue to partners that sell into Russia may have been negatively impacted due to the war in Ukraine." This is presented as a possible/potential effect that may have already occurred, so it is included per your instruction.

The filing discusses the separate U.S. export licensing requirements targeting China/Hong Kong/Macau (and Russia) for A100/H100 chips, systems, and A100X, and the requirement to transition certain operations out of China. Those China-focused restrictions are described as targeting "China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries" and are not attributed by the filing to the war in Ukraine, so I have not included them. Likewise, forward-looking statements (e.g., that the war "may continue" to impact EMEA sales, or that future sanctions/controls may be adopted) are excluded as future risks only.

## Effect of adopting the TDR accounting guidance on January 1, 2023

**1. Allowance for credit losses — net decrease of $587 million**

This is the cumulative-effect adjustment to the Firm's total allowance for credit losses recorded upon adoption of the new TDR guidance (ASU on Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings) under the modified retrospective method. It measures the reduction in the allowance resulting from the change in how allowances for modified loans to troubled borrowers are measured — the guidance eliminated TDR accounting and the requirement to use a discounted cash flow (DCF) methodology. JPMorgan elected its non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance approach for modified troubled loans in all portfolios except collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans (where it continued a DCF method, now using the post-modification rather than pre-modification effective interest rate).

Per the Note 13 allowance rollforward ("Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle"), the $587 million total decrease to the allowance for loan losses is broken down by portfolio segment as follows (in millions):
- **Consumer, excluding credit card: $(489) million decrease**
- **Credit card: $(100) million decrease**
- **Wholesale: $2 million increase**
- **Total: $(587) million net decrease** (Note 1 describes the decrease as "predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card")

**2. Retained earnings — increase of $446 million, after-tax**

This measures the after-tax cumulative-effect credit recorded directly to retained earnings on January 1, 2023 under the modified retrospective adoption. It is essentially the after-tax counterpart of the $587 million pre-tax release of the allowance for credit losses (i.e., the allowance reduction net of the related deferred income tax effect), recorded as an adjustment to opening retained earnings rather than through current-period earnings.

content:
Based on NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, the filing gives the following reasons why valuing non-marketable equity securities is complex and requires judgment:

1. **Absence of readily determinable fair values.** These are investments in privately-held companies that do not have a readily determinable fair value. They are measured at cost minus impairment, adjusted only for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment in the same issuer (the "measurement alternative").

2. **Lack of market prices and inherent illiquidity.** Fair value is based on observable inputs in an inactive market, and the filing states that "the valuation requires our judgment due to the absence of market prices and inherent lack of liquidity."

3. **Reliance on unobservable inputs.** The valuation methods incorporate unobservable inputs such as volatility, expected time to liquidity, the risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations — all of which require estimation.

4. **Judgmental impairment assessments.** NVIDIA assesses impairment quarterly based on both qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee's operating performance and market trends, which involves subjective evaluation. If impairment is identified, the investment must be written down to fair value with the charge recorded through Other income, net.

The filing also notes the materiality of these judgments: the carrying value of non-marketable equity securities grew from $3.4 billion at the end of fiscal 2025 to $22.3 billion at the end of fiscal 2026, with cumulative gross unrealized gains of $2.7 billion and cumulative gross unrealized losses and impairments of $176 million as of January 25, 2026.

Based on Pfizer's 2025 Form 10-K (Note 10, Identifiable Intangible Assets, and Note 4, Other (Income)/Deductions—Net), here is what the filing says about the change in IPR&D from $18.9 billion at year-end 2024 to $21.8 billion at year-end 2025:

**Causes of the change**

The 10-K states that the increase in the IPR&D gross carrying amount "primarily reflects $8.0 billion for the acquisition of Metsera" — the clinical-stage obesity/cardiometabolic company Pfizer acquired on November 13, 2025, for which it provisionally recorded $8.0 billion of identifiable intangible assets consisting of IPR&D (principally the MET-097i and MET-233i candidates). This addition was partially offset by:

1. **Impairments of $3.9 billion of IPR&D assets** (recorded in Other (income)/deductions—net; the filing's table shows $3,903 million of IPR&D impairment), and
2. **Transfers out of IPR&D to developed technology rights** — $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna), reflecting assets reclassified upon approval in a major market, at which point they begin to be amortized.

**Reasons given for the impairment charges**

The filing describes the 2025 intangible asset impairment charges ($4.9 billion total, associated with the Biopharma segment) as "primarily due to changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts." The IPR&D portion of $3.9 billion primarily included:

- **$1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin** (an IPR&D asset; the 2024 10-K had cited emerging competition for a prior impairment of this asset),
- **$820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib)**, and
- **$820 million for osivelotor** (the sickle cell disease candidate; elsewhere in the filing Pfizer notes the FDA placed osivelotor on a partial clinical hold, with permission later granted to resume certain studies).

In addition, the broader 2025 impairment total included about $1.0 billion of impairments "primarily for certain U.S. sterile injectable and hospital products" (covering developed technology rights, a finite-lived brand, and licensing agreements), but these did not affect the IPR&D line.

The filing also explains the methodology: impaired assets were written down to fair value using the income approach (multi-period excess earnings/discounted cash flow method), with key assumptions including the amount and timing of projected net cash flows (reflecting expected competitive, legal and regulatory forces), the probability of technical and regulatory success of ongoing clinical trials, the discount rate, and the tax rate. It cautions that IPR&D assets are high-risk given the uncertain nature of R&D and may become further impaired or written off in the future.

According to ExxonMobil's 2022 Form 10-K, the sharp rise in industry refining margins in 2022 was driven by a combination of demand recovery and constrained supply:

**Supply-side causes:**
- **Pandemic-driven refinery shutdowns and underinvestment** — Industry rationalization of refining assets took more than 3 million barrels per day of capacity offline, and investment had fallen below levels needed to maintain capacity (a trend that began pre-pandemic and accelerated during COVID-19), resulting in a tight market.
- **Supply chain constraints**, which added to the tightness across late 2021 and the first half of 2022.
- **Low inventory levels** (cited in the earnings factor analysis as contributing to the $14,360 million margin-driven earnings increase).

**Demand-side causes:**
- **Continued demand recovery** — Demand for gasoline and diesel recovered to pre-pandemic levels, while jet fuel demand remained below historical levels due to lingering COVID-19 impacts.

The net effect: "Refining margins increased sharply in 2022, well above the top of the 10-year historical range (2010–2019)." (Energy Products section, MD&A, p. 53 of the filing)

Based on a full review of all eight filings in the library, here are my findings.

## Filings that report an actual credit rating change during fiscal 2024

**1. JPMorgan Chase & Co. 2024 Form 10-K — Standard & Poor's (upgrade)**
In the "Credit ratings" section of the MD&A, the filing discloses that on November 15, 2024, Standard & Poor's upgraded the credit ratings of the parent company (JPMorgan Chase & Co., to long-term issuer A / short-term A-1), JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. (AA- / A-1+), J.P. Morgan Securities LLC, J.P. Morgan Securities plc and J.P. Morgan SE. S&P simultaneously revised its outlook on those entities from positive to stable. The same section notes that on November 11, 2024, Moody's affirmed all of those ratings (with outlook revisions only — stable to positive for the parent and certain subsidiaries, and negative to developing for the bank). Because the Moody's action was an affirmation with an outlook change rather than a change to the rating itself, only the S&P action qualifies as an upgrade.

**2. The Boeing Company 2024 Form 10-K — Moody's (downgrade)**
In the Capital Resources discussion, the filing states: "We currently maintain investment grade credit ratings; however, Moody's downgraded our short term and long term credit ratings to Baa3/P-3 in April 2024." The filing separately notes that Moody's and S&P placed Boeing's ratings on review for downgrade in September and October 2024, respectively, and that Moody's affirmed the Baa3/P-3 rating with a negative outlook in January 2025 — but those are review placements, an affirmation and an outlook action, not rating changes. Only the April 2024 Moody's downgrade qualifies.

## Filings with no reported rating change during the fiscal year

- **NVIDIA (FY ended Jan. 28, 2024):** Mentions credit rating changes only as a hypothetical risk factor ("Changes to our credit rating may negatively impact the value and liquidity of our securities..."). No actual rating action disclosed.

From Apple's fiscal 2024 Form 10-K (year ended September 28, 2024), here are the income tax payable/obligation balances as of that date, excluding the items you asked to omit.

**Balance sheet amounts (Note 6 – Consolidated Financial Statement Details, in millions):**

| Balance | Sept. 28, 2024 | What it represents |
|---|---|---|
| Income taxes payable — current (within Other current liabilities) | $26,601 | Income taxes owed and due within 12 months |
| Income taxes payable — non-current (within Other non-current liabilities) | $9,254 | Income taxes owed but not due within 12 months |
| **Total income taxes payable** | **$35,855** | Combined current and non-current balance |

**Components of those balances disclosed in MD&A (Liquidity and Capital Resources) and Note 7:**

1. **Deemed repatriation tax payable — $16.5 billion**, of which **$7.2 billion is expected to be paid within 12 months**. This is the remaining balance of the one-time transition tax imposed by the U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 on accumulated foreign earnings, which Apple is paying in installments. The current portion sits in current income taxes payable; the roughly $9.3 billion non-current portion corresponds to the non-current income taxes payable line above.

2. **State Aid Decision tax payable — €14.2 billion ($15.8 billion)**, all expected to be paid within 12 months. This is Apple's obligation to pay Ireland following the European Court of Justice's September 10, 2024 ruling confirming the European Commission's 2016 State Aid Decision (covering the period June 2003 through December 2014). The obligation will be settled via release of the escrow, and it is a component of the $26.6 billion current income taxes payable balance.

In short: the 10-K reports total income taxes payable of $35.855 billion at September 28, 2024 ($26.601 billion current, $9.254 billion non-current), with the two named obligations within that total being the $16.5 billion TCJA deemed repatriation tax and the $15.8 billion State Aid Decision payable to Ireland.

**787 Program abnormal production costs in Boeing's 2022 Form 10-K:**

1. **$1,240 million (i.e., $1.24 billion)** — Abnormal production costs **expensed during the year ended December 31, 2022**. Stated in Note 7 (Inventories): "We expensed abnormal production costs of $1,240 ... during the [year] ended December 31, 2022," and in the BCA MD&A: "Abnormal production costs in 2022 were $1,753 million, including $1,240 million related to the 787 program." 2. **$468 million** — Abnormal production costs **expensed during the year ended December 31, 2021** (comparative figure). Note 7: "We expensed abnormal production costs of $1,240 and $468 during the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021." These costs arose from abnormally low production rates plus excessive inspection and rework costs on inventoried aircraft.

3. **$1.7 billion** — **Cumulative abnormal costs recorded through December 31, 2022**. MD&A 787 Program Highlights: "Cumulative abnormal costs recorded through December 31, 2022 totaled $1.7 billion."

4. **$2.8 billion** — The **revised total estimate** of abnormal production costs, adjusted upward in Q4 2022, with most expected to be incurred by the end of 2023. MD&A: "During the fourth quarter of 2022 we adjusted the total estimate of abnormal production costs up to $2.8 billion with most being incurred by the end of 2023." The increase was driven by a Q4 2022 decision to slow near-term production due to supply chain constraints and increased inspection and rework costs.

5. **Approximately $2 billion** — The **prior cumulative estimate as of December 31, 2021** (the figure that was raised to $2.8 billion). MD&A: "At December 31, 2021, we were expecting to incur approximately $2 billion of abnormal production costs on a cumulative basis."

Context the filing provides: Boeing determined in Q3 2021 that 787 production rates below 5 per month were abnormally low, and that inspection/rework costs on inventoried aircraft were excessive; both categories are expensed as incurred as abnormal production costs. The filing provides the following context and reasons for this approach:

Because income taxes are explicitly embedded as a recoverable cost in regulated rate-setting, after-tax earnings are the economically meaningful measure of performance.

2. **Income taxes have an outsized and distorting effect on BHE's results.** The filing discloses that BHE's income tax line "includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation." These credits produce highly unusual negative effective tax rates (−81.6% in 2024, −215.1% in 2023, and −51.8% in 2022), causing net earnings after income taxes ($4.16 billion in 2024) to differ dramatically from pre-tax earnings ($2.29 billion in 2024). Evaluating BHE on a pre-tax basis would obscure this defining feature of the business.

In short, BHE is evaluated on earnings after income taxes because that is how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated, owing to the fact that income taxes (including substantial wind production tax credits) are a fundamental component of the regulated cost-of-service rate framework under which BHE operates.

Boeing's 2024 Form 10-K (BA_2024_10K.pdf) attributes the decline in commercial airplane deliveries (348 in 2024 vs. 528 in 2023) to the following causes, each of which the filing expressly links to deliveries:

1. The January 5, 2024 Alaska Airlines 737-9 accident and its aftermath. After the mid-exit door plug detached in flight, the FAA grounded the 737-9 fleet, investigated Boeing's (and Spirit AeroSystems') 737 quality control system, and increased oversight, capping 737 production at 38 per month and barring new production lines until quality and safety standards were met. As part of its resulting safety and quality plan, Boeing slowed production rates and delayed planned rate increases to reduce traveled work in its factory and at suppliers — actions the filing ties to lower 737 output and deliveries.

The strike that began September 13, 2024 paused production of the 737, 767, 777 and 777X (as well as commercial derivative defense aircraft) until a new contract was ratified in November, with production resuming in December. 3. 787 production and delivery constraints. Boeing slowed 787 production below 5 per month due to supply chain constraints and other production issues, and delays associated with business class seats "adversely impacted 2024 deliveries."

Flight-test delays and a revised assessment of certification timelines pushed the anticipated first 777-9 delivery to 2026, the 777-8 Freighter to 2028, and the 777-8 passenger aircraft to no earlier than 2030; Boeing also slowed the 777X production ramp, causing further customer delivery delays.
